title: To counter AI misinformation, invest in skills, literacy
where: The Ideas Page, page 9 (Tim Curtis, UNESCO)
syllabus: GS3 › Internal security: role of media and social networking sites; Cyber security; Science and technology: AI · GS2 › Important international institutions (UNESCO); Education (digital and media literacy); Elections · GS4 › Ethics in media and technology; Role of education in inculcating values
summary: UNESCO's South Asia head argues that laws and AI labels cannot keep pace with AI-made misinformation; India must build media and information literacy (MIL) for all, with platforms, newsrooms and creators sharing the job.
ideas: From access to judgement: generative AI makes convincing fakes cheap, so the question is no longer how to find information but how to judge what is reliable. Media and information literacy (MIL) is the answer.
GS3 · AI and misinformation
With generative AI making fakes cheap, the challenge has shifted from accessing information to judging it, which makes media and information literacy essential.
Connectivity is not capability: India has over a billion internet subscribers, but few can navigate the information space; platforms reward emotionally charged content, which deepens polarisation.
GS3 · Digital divide / social media
India's billion internet users show connectivity, not capability: only 18% of adults can file a cybercrime complaint online.
Misinformation does most harm in crises and elections, when people most need reliable information.
GS3 internal security · GS2 elections
Misinformation is most dangerous in crises and elections, as out-of-context flood videos in Nepal and a fake AI audio in Slovakia's election show.

Laws and labels are not enough: labelling AI content helps, but no law or detection tool can match the speed of synthetic content; people need skills, through trained teachers, local-language materials, and outreach beyond classrooms to rural people, women and persons with disabilities.
GS3 · Way forward / GS2 education
No law or detection tool can keep pace with AI fakes; lasting defence lies in citizens' skills, taught in local languages and beyond classrooms.

'We All Play a Part': platforms must be transparent about algorithms, label synthetic media and moderate beyond English and Hindi; newsrooms must explain how they verify; creators need verification skills and ethics.
GS3 governance · GS4 media ethics
Countering misinformation is a shared duty: transparent platforms, newsrooms that explain verification, and creators trained in ethics.
MIL is an investment in democracy: children grow up in AI-shaped feeds before they can question them, so MIL builds critical thinking, social trust and collective resilience.
GS2 democracy · Essay
Media literacy is not just safe technology use; it is an investment in critical thinking, social trust and democratic resilience.
keywords: Ability to access, understand, evaluate and share information responsibly
Media and information literacy is the most durable defence against AI-made misinformation.
AI that creates realistic text, images, audio and video
Generative AI has made synthetic media cheap and convincing.
AI-made fake audio or video of real people
A deepfake audio before Slovakia's 2023 election shows the threat to elections.
Labelling AI content helps but cannot stop deception or the misuse of genuine footage.
Platforms promoting content that grabs attention, often emotional
Platforms built for attention amplify emotionally charged and divisive content.
Content moderation beyond English and Hindi
Policing harmful content in all Indian languages
In multilingual India, moderation must work beyond English and Hindi.
Real evidence dismissed as fake because fakes are common
The spread of deepfakes lets people dismiss genuine footage as fake: the liar's dividend.
A society's shared ability to resist manipulation
MIL builds collective resilience against disinformation.

trend.t: Social media has moved through the papers from a tool of terror (ISIS recruitment 2015, non-state actors 2016) to a security challenge (social media and encryption 2024) to fake news and its regulation (IT Rules 2026). GS4 has added the ethics of social media (2025) and of AI (2024, 2026).
trend.watch: Social media and misinformation have come in four GS3 papers and in GS4 2025, and AI in 2023, 2024 and 2026. AI-driven misinformation joins both threads and is a must-study topic.

practice.q: Generative AI has made misinformation cheaper and faster. Discuss the threats it poses to democracy and internal security in India and suggest a strategy that goes beyond regulation.
parts: Introduction: generative AI and the misinformation challenge (one line, with facts)
Threats to democracy and internal security
Strategy beyond regulation (way forward, its own part)

answer.t: India has over a billion internet users (TRAI), yet only 18% of adults can file a cybercrime complaint online (NSO, 2025), and generative AI now makes convincing fakes cheap.

answer.h: Threats to democracy and internal security

pts.t: Deepfakes released just before polls can sway voters before they are debunked.
pts.ex: AI audio two days before Slovakia's 2023 election.

pts.t: Fabricated videos can spark violence within hours.
False content in crises misleads people when they most need facts.
Algorithms reward outrage, splitting society into hostile camps.
When fakes abound, genuine evidence is also doubted (the liar's dividend).
AI voice clones and fake identities enable scams.
Synthetic content spreads faster than any law or detection tool can act.
Labelling AI content cannot stop deception or the misuse of genuine footage.
Heavy regulation risks censorship of legitimate expression.
Moderation rarely works well beyond English and Hindi.
Content and platforms often lie outside Indian jurisdiction.
Many users cannot report or verify content.

pts.k: Media and information literacy in schools
pts.t: Teach students to evaluate sources, spot bias and understand algorithms, with trained teachers and local-language material.
Bring MIL to rural people, women and persons with disabilities.
Community radio, local journalists and health workers can share verified information, especially in emergencies.
Transparent algorithms, labelled synthetic media and rapid crisis response.

Government, platforms, media, schools and citizens each play a part.

answer.t: Laws can slow misinformation, but only a media-literate public can defeat it; MIL is an investment in democracy itself.

title: Israel polls: How its electoral system works and government is formed
syllabus: GS2 › Comparison of the Indian constitutional scheme with that of other countries; Salient features of the Representation of People's Act
summary: Israel elects a 120-member Knesset by nationwide proportional representation with a 3.25% threshold; no party has ever won a majority alone, so every government is a coalition.
evolution: Electoral threshold starts at 1%; raised to 1.5% (1992), 2% (2003) and 3.25% (2014).
Judicial reform debates, the October 7 attack and war shape politics.
Israel votes for the 26th Knesset, the first since 1988 to complete a full four-year term.
ideas: Parliamentary democracy with a unicameral legislature: a 120-member Knesset elected nationally for four years; the PM needs a working majority of 61.
GS2 · Comparative polity
Like India, Israel is a parliamentary democracy, but with a single-house, 120-member Knesset where the PM needs a 61-seat working majority.
Proportional representation by party lists, not first-past-the-post: seats match vote share, but a 3.25% threshold keeps out tiny parties.
GS2 · Electoral systems
Israel's list-based proportional representation, with a 3.25% threshold, contrasts with India's first-past-the-post system.
PR brings permanent coalitions: no party has ever won 61 seats alone, so small parties gain leverage and government formation takes time.
GS2 · Coalition politics
Proportional representation has made every Israeli government a coalition, giving small parties outsized leverage.
The President picks who forms the government (28 days plus 14), and a caretaker government continues if talks fail.
GS2 · Executive / President's role
Like India's President after a hung verdict, Israel's President invites the leader most likely to command a majority.
Parties can be disqualified for denying Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, racism or support for armed struggle (Section 7A, Basic Law: The Knesset).
GS2 · Elections / democracy
Israel's Section 7A lets its election body bar parties that deny the state or back armed struggle.
keywords: Unlike India's bicameral Parliament, Israel has a single-house Knesset.
Seats in proportion to votes for party lists
Israel uses nationwide party-list proportional representation; India uses first-past-the-post.
Minimum vote share to win seats (3.25% in Israel)
A 3.25% threshold balances representation with stability.
Support of at least 61 of 120 members
An Israeli government must keep a 61-seat working majority.
Votes for parties below the threshold, reallocated to others
Votes for parties below 3.25% become wasted votes.
Government formed by several parties together
Every Israeli government has been a coalition.
Outgoing government that runs affairs till a new one is formed
If talks fail, a caretaker government under the current PM continues.
Israel's set of constitutional laws in place of a single written constitution
Israel has Basic Laws instead of a single written constitution like India's.
Israel's election body (compare Election Commission of India)
Israel's Central Elections Committee, like India's Election Commission, runs national elections.
data: Israel's electoral threshold, giving at least 4 of 120 seats
Israel's 3.25% threshold guarantees a qualifying party at least four of 120 seats.
An Israeli government needs at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats.
examples: Israel's 2026 election
38 parties contest; about 11 expected to clear the threshold
PR and fragmentation
In 2026, 38 parties contested but only about 11 were expected to win seats.
Mergers before polls
The high threshold pushes small parties into joint lists
Effects of a threshold
Israel's threshold pushes small factions into joint slates, as seen in 2026.
pyqs: Comparison of systems: India's parliamentary model versus others; Israel shows a pure parliamentary model with PR.
Parliamentary sovereignty compared: Israel, without a single written constitution, is closer to the British model.
Basic tenets of democracies compared; Israel adds a proportional-representation contrast.
Equality in constitutions compared; Israel's 'Jewish and democratic' identity is a contrast.
India–Israel ties (I2U2): knowing Israel's politics helps answer foreign-policy questions.

The questions compare specific features: separation of powers, pardon, equality, secularism, parliamentary sovereignty, judicial appointments.
trend.watch: A comparison question has come almost every year since 2021, mostly with the US and UK. Prominent elections abroad (Israel now) make other systems likely: study comparisons by feature.

practice.q: Compare the parliamentary democracies of India and Israel with reference to their legislature, executive, judiciary and electoral systems.
parts: Introduction: both parliamentary democracies, Israel just voted (one line, with facts)
Electoral system and nature of democracy

answer.t: India and Israel are both parliamentary democracies, but Israel's 27 October 2026 election, under proportional representation, shows how differently they work.

pts.t: India is bicameral (Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha); Israel's Knesset is unicameral with 120 members.
Both elect the lower house for a fixed term, five years in India and four in Israel.
pts.ex: The 2026 Knesset is the first since 1988 to complete its term.

pts.t: India's Rajya Sabha represents states; Israel, a unitary state, has no such house.
In both, the PM leads and must keep the confidence of the house.
Both Presidents are largely ceremonial but invite the leader most likely to form a government.
Every Israeli government has been a coalition; India has had both single-party and coalition governments.
Both allow caretaker governments until a new one is formed.
India has a single written constitution; Israel relies on Basic Laws.
India's courts can strike down even amendments under the basic structure doctrine; Israel's Supreme Court interprets Basic Laws.
Both have seen debates over the judiciary's power.

answer.h: Electoral system and nature of democracy

pts.t: India uses first-past-the-post in constituencies; Israel uses nationwide party-list PR.
Israel needs 3.25% to win seats; India has no threshold.
PR gives small parties a voice but also leverage; FPTP gives stabler majorities.
India's Election Commission and Israel's Central Elections Committee run polls.
Israel can bar parties under Section 7A; India deregisters parties on narrower grounds.
Both have universal adult franchise.

answer.t: Israel shows PR's gain in representation and its cost in stability; India's FPTP, with a written constitution and strong judicial review, trades some representation for stable government.
